title: Properties of Logarithms & Solving Exponential/Logarithmic Equations
learningObjective: EL5: Use properties of logarithms to condense or expand logarithmic expressions. EL6: Solve exponential and logarithmic equations.

faqs.question: What is the one-to-one property of logarithms, and why does it work?
faqs.answer:
The one-to-one property says that if two logarithms with the SAME base are equal, then their arguments must be equal too: \( \log_b(M) = \log_b(N) \) if and only if \( M = N \) (for positive \( M \) and \( N \)). This works because a logarithmic function is one-to-one (FN6) — each output comes from exactly one input — so if two logs with the same base produce the same output, they had to start from the same input.
Example

If \( \log_3(x) = \log_3(7) \), then \( x=7 \).

faqs.question: What is the product property of logarithms, and where does it come from?
faqs.answer:
The product property turns the logarithm of a product into a sum of two separate logarithms.
Formula

\[ \log_b(m \cdot n) = \log_b(m) + \log_b(n) \]

(for positive \( m \) and \( n \))

This comes directly from the exponent rule \( b^x \cdot b^y = b^{x+y} \) — since logarithms ARE exponents (EL3), multiplying two numbers corresponds to adding their exponents, which is exactly what this property captures.

faqs.question: What is the quotient property of logarithms?
faqs.answer:
The quotient property turns the logarithm of a fraction into a difference of two separate logarithms — the mirror image of the product property.
Formula

\[ \log_a\left(\dfrac{m}{n}\right) = \log_a(m) - \log_a(n) \]

(for positive \( m \) and \( n \))

faqs.question: What is the power property of logarithms?
faqs.answer:
The power property lets you move an exponent from inside a logarithm's argument out in front, as a multiplier.
Formula

\[ \log_a(m^n) = n \cdot \log_a(m) \]

(for positive \( m \))

This is one of the most useful properties for solving equations, since it's the tool that lets you "bring down" an exponent you're trying to solve for.

faqs.question: What is the change of base formula, and when would I need it?
faqs.answer:
Extension (beyond the EL5 CheckIt exercise). The change of base formula rewrites a logarithm with any base as a ratio of two logarithms in a DIFFERENT, more convenient base — usually base 10 or base e, since those are the only two bases most calculators have a dedicated button for.
Formula

\[ \log_a(x) = \dfrac{\log_b(x)}{\log_b(a)} \]

(b can be any valid base — commonly 10 or e)

faqs.question: What does it mean to "expand" versus "condense" a logarithmic expression?
faqs.answer: Expanding means breaking one logarithm containing a product, quotient, or exponent into several simpler logarithms added or subtracted together. Condensing means running that process backward — combining several separate logarithms into a single logarithm. They're opposite skills using the exact same three properties (product, quotient, power), just applied in opposite directions.

faqs.question: How do I expand a logarithmic expression using the product, quotient, and power properties?
faqs.answer:
Work from the outside in: identify the overall structure first (is the whole thing a product, a quotient, or something raised to a power?), apply the matching property to split it into pieces, then repeat on any pieces that still have more than one factor.
Worked Example

Expand \( \log_2\left(\dfrac{x^3 y}{z}\right) \).

Quotient property: \( \log_2(x^3y) - \log_2(z) \)

Product property: \( \log_2(x^3) + \log_2(y) - \log_2(z) \)

Power property: \( 3\log_2(x) + \log_2(y) - \log_2(z) \)

faqs.question: How do I condense multiple logarithms into a single logarithm?
faqs.answer:
Run the expanding process in reverse: handle any coefficients in front of a logarithm first by moving them back up as exponents (power property backward), then combine addition into a product and subtraction into a quotient.
Worked Example

Condense \( 2\log(x) + \log(y) - \log(z) \).

Power property backward: \( \log(x^2) + \log(y) - \log(z) \)

Product then quotient: \( \log\left(\dfrac{x^2y}{z}\right) \)

faqs.question: How do I solve an exponential equation when both sides already have the same base?
faqs.answer:
Extension (beyond the EL6 CheckIt exercise). Use the one-to-one property of exponentials: if the bases match (a positive base other than 1), you can simply set the exponents equal to each other and solve — no logarithms needed at all.
Worked Example

Solve \( 5^{3x} = 5^{7x-2} \).

Same base, so set exponents equal: \( 3x = 7x-2 \)

Solve: \( -4x=-2 \) → \( x=\dfrac{1}{2} \)

faqs.question: How do I solve an exponential equation when the two sides have different bases?
faqs.answer: Extension (beyond the EL6 CheckIt exercise). First check whether you can rewrite both sides using a common base (like rewriting 4 as \( 2^2 \)); if so, set the exponents equal (see "How do I solve an exponential equation when both sides already have the same base?"). If the bases can't be matched, take the logarithm of both sides instead (see "How do I solve an exponential equation using the 'take the log of both sides' method?").

faqs.question: How do I solve an exponential equation using the "take the log of both sides" method?
faqs.answer:
Take log (or ln) of both sides, use the power property to bring the exponent down as a multiplier, then solve the resulting equation algebraically for the variable.
Worked Example

Solve \( 3^x = 7 \).

Take log of both sides: \( \log(3^x) = \log(7) \)

Power property: \( x\log(3) = \log(7) \)

Solve: \( x = \dfrac{\log(7)}{\log(3)} \approx 1.7712 \)

For CheckIt's equations, switching to log form gives the same answer in the exact form CheckIt shows: \( x=\log_3 7 \).

faqs.question: How do I solve a logarithmic equation by condensing it into a single logarithm first?
faqs.answer:
Extension (beyond the EL6 CheckIt exercise). Condense the equation into the form \( \log_b(\text{something}) = \text{a number} \), then convert to exponential form (EL3) and solve algebraically.
Worked Example

Solve \( \log_2(x) + \log_2(x-2) = 3 \).

Condense: \( \log_2(x(x-2)) = 3 \)

Convert to exponential form: \( x(x-2) = 2^3 = 8 \)

Solve the resulting quadratic: \( x^2-2x-8=0 \) → \( x=4 \) or \( x=-2 \)

Not done yet: \( x=-2 \) makes \( \log_2(-2) \) undefined, so reject it (see the next question). The solution is \( x=4 \).

faqs.question: How do I check for extraneous solutions when solving a logarithmic equation?
faqs.answer:
Extension (beyond the EL6 CheckIt exercise). Plug every candidate solution back into the ORIGINAL equation (before you condensed or converted anything) and confirm every logarithm's argument comes out positive and that the equation is true. Since a logarithm's domain requires a positive argument (EL4), any solution that makes an argument zero or negative must be thrown out — even though it solved the condensed algebraic equation correctly.
Worked Example

From the condensing example above: candidates \( x=4 \) and \( x=-2 \).

Check \( x=-2 \) in the original: \( \log_2(-2) \) — argument is negative, undefined.

Reject \( x=-2 \). Only \( x=4 \) is a valid solution.

faqs.question: How do I use the change of base formula to evaluate a logarithm on a calculator?
faqs.answer:
Extension (beyond the EL5 CheckIt exercise). Rewrite the logarithm as a fraction of two common (or natural) logarithms using the change of base formula (see the change of base question above), then evaluate each one on a calculator and divide.
Worked Example

Evaluate \( \log_5(30) \).

Change of base: \( \dfrac{\log(30)}{\log(5)} \)

\( \approx \dfrac{1.477}{0.699} \approx 2.113 \)

(Rounding only at the end gives the same 2.113.)

faqs.question: How do the properties of logarithms in EL5 make solving equations possible in EL6?
faqs.answer: EL5's properties are what make the harder equations possible. The power property is what lets you bring an exponent down if you take a log of both sides. The product and quotient properties let you condense an equation with several logs into the single \( \log_b(\text{something}) = \text{number} \) form before you switch to exponential form. The EL6 CheckIt equations have only one log or one power, so you can solve them with just the switch between forms from EL3. The EL5 properties come into play when there is more than one log, or different bases on each side.

faqs.question: How does this section connect back to EL1–EL4?
faqs.answer: Every piece of this section leans on something earlier in the unit. EL1 and EL3 gave you the exponential and logarithmic definitions these properties are built from. EL4's domain rule (a logarithm's input must be positive) is exactly why you have to check for extraneous solutions (see "How do I check for extraneous solutions…") — a candidate solution isn't valid unless it actually lands inside the function's domain. This section is less a brand-new topic and more the payoff of everything the unit has been building toward.

faqs.question: Why do these equation-solving skills matter beyond this course?
faqs.answer: Solving exponential and logarithmic equations is the essential skill behind answering real questions like "how long until this investment doubles," "how long until this radioactive sample decays to half its original amount," or "how many years until a population reaches a certain size." Anywhere a real-world exponential model shows up, eventually you need to solve for the input — and that's exactly the skill this section builds.

guided.title: Practice Expanding Logarithmic Expressions
guided.prompt: I'm practicing EL5: expanding a logarithm and naming the property I use at each step. Give me one problem shaped like my CheckIt exercise: log base b of a fraction, where b is a whole number from 2 to 9, the numerator has exactly one letter and the denominator has exactly two different letters, and each letter has a different whole-number exponent from 2 to 7. For example, log_3( x^4 / (y^2 z^5) ), but use different letters and numbers. Assume every letter stands for a positive number. Don't solve it yet. I'll write my steps and name the property at each one (product rule, quotient rule, or power rule). Then show your own step-by-step expansion, but make exactly one deliberate mistake: when you split the log of the denominator's product, write the second denominator term with a plus sign instead of a minus sign. Don't tell me where the mistake is. I'll compare your work with mine, find it, and explain why the minus sign has to reach both denominator terms. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Practice Condensing Logarithmic Expressions
guided.prompt: I'm practicing EL5: condensing several logarithms into one and naming the property I use at each step. Give me one expression shaped like my CheckIt exercise: three logs with the same base b (a whole number from 2 to 9), three different letters, and coefficients that are three different whole numbers from 2 to 7, at least one of them negative. For example, 5 log_2 k - 7 log_2 t + 6 log_2 n, but use different letters and numbers. Assume every letter is positive. Don't solve it yet. I'll condense it myself, naming the property at each step (power rule first, then product and quotient). Then show your own step-by-step solution, but make exactly one deliberate mistake: put the letter from a term with a negative coefficient in the numerator instead of the denominator. Don't tell me where it is. I'll find it, and I'll test it by checking that your final single log and the original expression can't be equal. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Practice Solving CheckIt-Style Exponential Equations
guided.prompt: I'm practicing EL6: solving exponential equations with exact answers. Give me a pair of equations shaped like my CheckIt exercise, using the same three numbers in both: b^(x - a) = c and b^x - a = c, where b is a whole number from 2 to 5 and a and c are different whole numbers from 2 to 9. For example, 3^(x - 6) = 2 and 3^x - 6 = 2, but use different numbers. Don't solve them yet. I'll solve both, leaving my answers exact (like log_3(2) + 6). Then show your solutions, but make exactly one deliberate mistake: in the second equation, switch to log form before adding a, so you write x - a = log_b c. Don't tell me which one has the mistake. I'll find it, and I'll check both of your answers by turning them into decimals on my calculator and substituting them back into the original equations. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Extension: Checking for Extraneous Solutions (beyond the EL6 CheckIt exercise)
guided.prompt: This is an extension beyond my EL6 CheckIt exercise. I'm learning to solve log equations with two logs and to check for extraneous solutions. Give me an equation of the form log_b(x) + log_b(x + k) = n, where b, k and n are positive whole numbers chosen so that x(x + k) = b^n factors into two whole-number solutions. For example, log_2(x) + log_2(x - 2) = 3 is the same idea, but use a plus sign and different numbers. Don't solve it yet. I'll condense it, switch forms, solve the quadratic, and test each candidate in the ORIGINAL equation. Then show your solution, but make exactly one deliberate mistake: keep the negative candidate as a valid answer. Don't point it out. I'll find it by substituting into the original logs and saying which input becomes negative. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

guided.title: Extension: Where EL5's Properties Show Up in EL6
guided.prompt: This is an extension beyond my EL5 and EL6 CheckIt exercises. Give me two log equations. The first should be CheckIt-style: a log_b(cx) = ad, where b is a whole number from 2 to 5, a and c are different whole numbers from 2 to 9, and d is 2 or 3. The second should be log_b(x) + log_b(x + k) = n, with whole numbers chosen so that x(x + k) = b^n has whole-number solutions. Before solving, tell me which EL5 property (product, quotient or power rule), if any, each equation needs, and why. Make exactly one deliberate mistake in what you claim: say that the second equation is condensed with the quotient rule. I'll check your claims against my class notes, say which equation needs no EL5 property at all, and correct the wrong claim. Then I'll solve both. After I respond, check my reasoning and give me the fully corrected solution before we finish.

stages.desc: Two quick reviews EL5 leans on: exponent rules and logs as exponents (EL3). Skip any you already have.

stops.title: Exponent rules
stops.target: Use the three exponent rules: \(b^m b^n = b^{m+n}\), \(\dfrac{b^m}{b^n} = b^{m-n}\), \((b^m)^p = b^{mp}\). Also move factors with negative exponents across the fraction bar: \(y^{-5} = \dfrac{1}{y^5}\).
stops.cold: Simplify (a) \(x^3 \cdot x^4\) (b) \(\dfrac{x^7}{x^2}\) (c) \((x^3)^4\). Then (d) write \(x^3 y^{-5}\) as a fraction with positive exponents.
stops.coldPlain: Simplify (a) x^3 * x^4, (b) x^7/x^2, (c) (x^3)^4. Then (d) write x^3 y^(-5) as a fraction with positive exponents.
stops.solution: Multiplying powers of the same base adds exponents; dividing subtracts; a power of a power multiplies. A negative exponent means the factor belongs in the denominator: y^(-5) = 1/y^5.
stops.mistake: Multiplying exponents in (a) or dividing them in (b).
stops.again: Write \(\dfrac{n^6}{m^2 k^3}\) as a product with no fraction bar, using negative exponents.
stops.reflect: Which operation on powers turns into addition of exponents?

stops.title: Logs of powers
stops.target: Remember from EL3: a log is an exponent, so \(\log_b(b^k) = k\).
stops.cold: Evaluate \(\log_2(2^5)\), \(\log_2 8\), and \(\log_2 4\). What do you notice about \(\log_2(8 \cdot 4)\)?
stops.coldPlain: Evaluate log_2(2^5), log_2 8, and log_2 4. What do you notice about log_2(8 * 4)?
stops.coldA: \(5\), \(3\), \(2\). And \(\log_2(8 \cdot 4) = \log_2 32 = 5 = 3 + 2\): the log of a product is the sum of the logs. That pattern is the next stop.
stops.solution: log_2(2^5) = 5 because the log is the exponent. log_2 8 = 3 and log_2 4 = 2. 8 * 4 = 32 = 2^5, so log_2(32) = 5 = 3 + 2. Multiplying inside became adding outside, because 2^3 * 2^2 = 2^(3+2).
stops.againA: \(4\), \(2\), and \(\log_3 9 = 2 = 4 - 2\). Dividing inside became subtracting outside.
stops.reflect: Why would multiplying inside a log turn into adding outside it?

stages.desc: The three properties and where they come from, then expanding and condensing (the EL5 check), common mistakes, and change of base.

stops.title: Product and quotient rules
stops.target: \(\log_b(MN) = \log_b M + \log_b N\) and \(\log_b\left(\dfrac{M}{N}\right) = \log_b M - \log_b N\). A log is an exponent, so the exponent rules become log rules.
stops.explain:
Where the properties come from

Each log property is an exponent rule in disguise, because a log is an exponent.

[[graph:RULES]]
stops.coldA: \(\log_4 m + \log_4 n\) (product rule) and \(\log_4 m - \log_4 n\) (quotient rule).
stops.solution: A product inside becomes a sum of logs (product rule). A quotient inside becomes a difference: numerator minus denominator (quotient rule).
stops.mistake: Writing log_4(m/n) as log_4 m / log_4 n.
stops.reflect: Which exponent rule is the product rule really using?

stops.title: Power rule
stops.target: \(\log_b(M^p) = p\log_b M\): an exponent inside the log moves to the front as a coefficient.
stops.coldA: \(4\log_6 w\) and \(-5\log_9 k\). Negative exponents come out as negative coefficients.
stops.solution: The power rule moves the exponent to the front: log_6(w^4) = 4 log_6 w; log_9(k^(-5)) = -5 log_9 k.
stops.mistake: Writing (log_6 w)^4, which is a different thing.
stops.again: Extension (beyond the EL5 CheckIt exercise) for the first one: Expand \(\log(\sqrt{x})\) and \(\log_4\left(\dfrac{1}{z^2}\right)\).
stops.againA: \(\sqrt{x} = x^{1/2}\), so \(\tfrac{1}{2}\log x\). \(\dfrac{1}{z^2} = z^{-2}\), so \(-2\log_4 z\). (Both need \(x > 0\) and \(z > 0\); for any \(z \ne 0\), \(\log_4\left(\tfrac{1}{z^2}\right) = -2\log_4|z|\).)
stops.reflect: What is the difference between \(\log(x^5)\) and \((\log x)^5\)?

stops.title: Expand step by step
stops.target: Expand one log into sums and differences, one property per step, and name the property each time: quotient, then product, then power.
stops.cold: Expand \(\log_9\left(\dfrac{k^2 n^6}{t^3}\right)\), naming the property at each step.
stops.coldPlain: Expand log_9( k^2 n^6 / t^3 ), naming the property at each step.
stops.note: Show every step and name the log property (product, quotient, or power rule) you used at each step. Check that I named the right property each time.
stops.solution: Step 1, quotient rule: log_9(k^2 n^6) - log_9(t^3). Step 2, product rule: log_9(k^2) + log_9(n^6) - log_9(t^3). Step 3, power rule: 2 log_9 k + 6 log_9 n - 3 log_9 t.
stops.mistake: Applying the power rule to the whole fraction, or (when the denominator has two factors) subtracting only the first one.
stops.again: Expand \(\log_5\left(\dfrac{s^4}{m^2 y^7}\right)\), naming each property. (CheckIt shows its expand problem as a fraction like this one.)
stops.againA: Final answer: \(4\log_5 s - 2\log_5 m - 7\log_5 y\). The minus sign in front of the denominator's log reaches both factors in the denominator.[[graph:EX2]]
stops.stretch: Extension, beyond the EL5 CheckIt exercise: Expand \(\log_2\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{x}}{y^3}\right)\).
stops.reflect: Why does the quotient rule usually come first when expanding?

stops.title: Condense step by step
stops.target: Condense a sum and difference of logs into one log by running the properties backward: power first (coefficients become exponents), then product and quotient.
stops.cold: Condense \(4\log_7 d - 6\log_7 s + 2\log_7 w\), naming the property at each step.
stops.coldPlain: Condense 4 log_7 d - 6 log_7 s + 2 log_7 w, naming the property at each step.
stops.note: Show every step and name the log property (product, quotient, or power rule) you used at each step. Check that I named the right property each time.
stops.solution: Step 1, power rule backward: log_7(d^4) - log_7(s^6) + log_7(w^2). Step 2, product rule: log_7(d^4 w^2) - log_7(s^6). Step 3, quotient rule: log_7(d^4 w^2 / s^6).
stops.mistake: Combining before moving the coefficients up, which leaves a 4 or 6 stranded outside the log.
stops.reflect: Why must the coefficients move up first?

stops.title: Common mistakes
stops.target: The properties only work for products, quotients, and powers inside one log. \(\log(x + y)\) cannot be split, and \(\dfrac{\log x}{\log y}\) is not \(\log\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right)\).
stops.cold:
True or false? Test each with \(x = 10\), \(y = 100\) and base-10 logs.
(a) \(\log(x + y) = \log x + \log y\) (b) \(\log(xy) = \log x + \log y\) (c) \(\dfrac{\log x}{\log y} = \log\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right)\) (d) \((\log x)^2 = 2\log x\)
stops.coldPlain: True or false, testing with x = 10, y = 100, base-10 logs: (a) log(x + y) = log x + log y; (b) log(xy) = log x + log y; (c) log x / log y = log(x/y); (d) (log x)^2 = 2 log x.
stops.coldA: (a) False: \(\log 110 \approx 2.04\), but \(1 + 2 = 3\). (b) True: \(\log 1000 = 3 = 1 + 2\). (c) False: \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) vs. \(\log 0.1 = -1\). (d) False: \((\log 10)^2 = 1\), but \(2\log 10 = 2\). The power rule is \(\log(x^2) = 2\log x\) (for \(x > 0\)), with the exponent inside.
stops.solution: (a) log 110 is about 2.04, not 3, so false: there is no rule for a sum inside a log. (b) True, the product rule. (c) log 10 / log 100 = 1/2, but log(0.1) = -1, so false. (d) (log 10)^2 = 1 but 2 log 10 = 2, so false: the power rule needs the exponent inside the log: log(x^2) = 2 log x for x > 0.
stops.mistake: Splitting log(x + y) into log x + log y.
stops.again: Can \(\log_3(9 + 27)\) be simplified with a log property? Can \(\log_3(9 \cdot 27)\)?
stops.againA: \(\log_3(9 + 27) = \log_3 36\): no property applies to a sum. \(\log_3(9 \cdot 27) = \log_3 9 + \log_3 27 = 2 + 3 = 5\).
stops.reflect: What is the quickest way to test whether a "rule" you remember is real?

stops.title: Change of base (extension, beyond the EL5 CheckIt exercise)
stops.target: \(\log_b a = \dfrac{\ln a}{\ln b} = \dfrac{\log a}{\log b}\). Use it to evaluate any log on a calculator.
stops.explain:
Why change of base works

Let \(c = \log_3 20\). That means \(3^c = 20\). Take \(\ln\) of both sides: \(\ln(3^c) = \ln 20\). The power rule gives \(c \ln 3 = \ln 20\), so \(c = \dfrac{\ln 20}{\ln 3}\). The same steps work for any base.
stops.cold: Use change of base to evaluate \(\log_3 20\) to four decimal places.
stops.coldPlain: Use change of base to evaluate log_3 20 to four decimal places.
stops.solution: log_3 20 = ln 20 / ln 3, about 2.7268. It makes sense: 3^2 = 9 and 3^3 = 27, so the answer must be between 2 and 3.
stops.mistake: Dividing in the wrong order (ln 3 / ln 20), or computing ln(20/3).
stops.again: Evaluate \(\log_7 50\) to four decimal places. Estimate first.
stops.againA: \(7^2 = 49\), so it should be just over 2. \(\dfrac{\ln 50}{\ln 7} \approx 2.0104\).
stops.stretch: Rewrite \(y = \log_2 x\) so you could type it into a calculator that only has \(\ln\).
stops.reflect: How can you estimate a log before using change of base, to check your answer?

stages.desc: A practice check in the EL5 CheckIt format (expand and condense, naming each property), plus change of base.

stops.title: Practice check
stops.target: Expand and condense logarithmic expressions step by step, naming each property, and use change of base.
stops.cold:
(1) Demonstrate step-by-step how to expand \(\log_7\left(\dfrac{m^4 s^2}{w^3}\right)\), explaining the logarithm property you are using each step.
(2) Demonstrate step-by-step how to condense \(5\log_2 k - 7\log_2 t + 6\log_2 n\), explaining the logarithm property you are using each step.
(3) Extension, beyond the EL5 CheckIt exercise: evaluate \(\log_4 30\) to four decimal places.
stops.coldPlain: (1) Expand log_7( m^4 s^2 / w^3 ) step by step, naming each property. (2) Condense 5 log_2 k - 7 log_2 t + 6 log_2 n step by step, naming each property. (3) Extension: evaluate log_4 30 to four decimal places.
stops.note: Show every step and name the log property (product, quotient, or power rule) you used at each step. Check that I named the right property each time.
stops.solution: (1) Quotient rule: log_7(m^4 s^2) - log_7(w^3); product rule: log_7(m^4) + log_7(s^2) - log_7(w^3); power rule: 4 log_7 m + 2 log_7 s - 3 log_7 w. (2) Power rule backward: log_2(k^5) - log_2(t^7) + log_2(n^6); product rule: log_2(k^5 n^6) - log_2(t^7); quotient rule: log_2(k^5 n^6 / t^7). (3) ln 30 / ln 4 is about 2.4534 (between 2 and 3, since 4^2 = 16 and 4^3 = 64).
stops.mistake: Not naming the property at each step; the check asks for it.
stops.again:
(1) Expand \(\log_8\left(\dfrac{x^5}{a^2 d^6}\right)\), naming each property.
(2) Condense \(-3\log_6 y + 7\log_6 z - 4\log_6 b\), naming each property.
(3) Extension, beyond the EL5 CheckIt exercise: evaluate \(\log_9 2\) to four decimal places.
stops.againA: (1) \(5\log_8 x - 2\log_8 a - 6\log_8 d\)[[graph:F2a]](2) \(\log_6\left(\dfrac{z^7}{y^3 b^4}\right)\)[[graph:F2b]](3) \(\dfrac{\ln 2}{\ln 9} \approx 0.3155\) (less than 1, since 2 is less than 9)
stops.reflect: Which direction (expanding or condensing) is harder for you, and which property trips you up?

paths.label: EL6: Solving Exponential and Log Equations
paths.sectionLabel: EL6, Solving Exponential and Logarithmic Equations
paths.intro: Builds to the EL6 check: solving exponential and logarithmic equations, plus same-base equations, taking ln of both sides, and checking for extraneous solutions. Practice scope: the EL6 CheckIt exercise gives four equations (two exponential, two logarithmic) with exact answers; same-base equations, taking ln of both sides, base e, decimals, and equations with several logs (extraneous solutions) are extensions.

stages.desc: Two quick reviews EL6 leans on: converting forms (EL3) and condensing (EL5). Skip any you already have.

stops.title: Switch between log and exponential form
stops.target: Recall from EL3: \(b^c = a\) and \(\log_b a = c\) say the same thing.
stops.cold: Rewrite \(2^x = 7\) in log form, and \(\log_3 x = 4\) in exponential form.
stops.coldPlain: Rewrite 2^x = 7 in log form, and log_3 x = 4 in exponential form.
stops.solution: 2^x = 7: base 2, exponent x, result 7, so x = log_2 7. log_3 x = 4: base 3, exponent 4, so x = 3^4 = 81.
stops.mistake: Writing x = log_7 2 (swapping base and result).
stops.reflect: Converting is what "undoes" an exponent or a log. Why is that useful for solving?

stops.title: Condense logs
stops.target: Recall from EL5: combine \(\log_b M + \log_b N\) into \(\log_b(MN)\) and \(\log_b M - \log_b N\) into \(\log_b\left(\tfrac{M}{N}\right)\).
stops.coldA: \(\log_2\big(x(x - 2)\big)\), or \(\log_2(x^2 - 2x)\), for \(x > 2\). The condensed form is also defined for \(x < 0\), but the original is not, which is where extraneous answers come from.
stops.solution: Product rule: a sum of logs with the same base is the log of the product: log_2(x(x - 2)).
stops.againA: \(\ln\left(\dfrac{x + 1}{x - 1}\right)\), for \(x > 1\) (where both original logs are defined).
stops.reflect: Why would you want an equation to have only one log in it?

stages.desc: Exponential equations first, then log equations. The big habit: isolate the power or the log, then convert.

stops.title: Same base on both sides (extension, beyond the EL6 CheckIt exercise)
stops.target: If both sides can be written as powers of the same base \(b\) (with \(b > 0\), \(b \ne 1\)), set the exponents equal: \(b^m = b^n\) means \(m = n\).
stops.solution: Write 8 as 2^3, then match exponents: x + 1 = 3, x = 2. For 9^x = 27, rewrite both with base 3: 3^(2x) = 3^3, so 2x = 3 and x = 3/2.
stops.reflect: When does the same-base method not work?

stops.title: Exponential equations: isolate, then convert
stops.target: When the bases cannot match, get the power alone, then rewrite in log form. Give the exact answer as a log, then a decimal with change of base. CheckIt wants only the exact answer; the decimal is a check.
stops.cold: Solve \(3^{x - 6} = 2\) and \(3^x - 6 = 2\). Give exact answers, then decimals to check them.
stops.coldPlain: Solve 3^(x - 6) = 2 and 3^x - 6 = 2. Give exact answers, then decimals to check them.
stops.coldA: [[graph:S1]]The graph shows the same answer: the curve \(y = 3^{x-6}\) meets the line \(y = 2\) at \(x \approx 6.63\).[[graph:I1]][[graph:S2]]
stops.solution: 3^(x - 6) = 2: the power is alone, so x - 6 = log_3 2, and x = log_3 2 + 6, about 6.6309. 3^x - 6 = 2: add 6 first, 3^x = 8, so x = log_3 8, about 1.8928. Same base and same numbers, but different answers, because the 6 is in a different place.
stops.mistake: Switching forms before the power is alone, like writing x - 6 = log_3 2 for 3^x - 6 = 2.
stops.reflect: Why must the power be alone before you convert?

stops.title: Take ln of both sides (extension, beyond the EL6 CheckIt exercise)
stops.target: Another route: take \(\ln\) of both sides and use the power rule to bring the exponent down. This is the go-to move for base \(e\) and for different bases on each side.
stops.solution: ln(3^x) = ln 20 becomes x ln 3 = ln 20 by the power rule, so x = ln 20 / ln 3 (the same as log_3 20). For e^(2x) = 9: ln(e^(2x)) = 2x, so 2x = ln 9 and x = ln 9 / 2.
stops.reflect: How is taking ln of both sides the same as using change of base?

stops.title: Log equations: isolate, then convert
stops.target: Get the log alone, rewrite in exponential form, solve, and check that the argument is positive.
stops.solution: 6 log_2(4x) = 18: divide by 6, log_2(4x) = 3, so 4x = 2^3 = 8 and x = 2. 6 + log_2(4y) = 8: subtract 6, log_2(4y) = 2, so 4y = 4 and y = 1. Both inside values (8 and 4) are positive. A whole-number answer is fine; CheckIt often has them.
stops.mistake: Converting before isolating, like writing 4x = 2^18 for 6 log_2(4x) = 18.
stops.reflect: What is the same about the first move in exponential and log equations?

stops.title: Combine logs and check for extraneous solutions (extension, beyond the EL6 CheckIt exercise)
stops.target: With more than one log, condense first (EL5), convert, solve, and then check every answer: any answer that puts a non-positive number inside a log is extraneous.
stops.coldA: Only \(x = 4\) works.[[graph:S5]]The graph agrees: the left side exists only for \(x > 2\) and keeps increasing there, so it crosses \(y = 3\) exactly once, at \(x = 4\). The value \(x = -2\) is not even in its domain.[[graph:I5]]
stops.solution: Condense: log_2(x(x - 2)) = 3. Convert: x(x - 2) = 8, so x^2 - 2x - 8 = 0, (x - 4)(x + 2) = 0. x = -2 makes log_2(-2) undefined, so reject it. x = 4: log_2 4 + log_2 2 = 3, correct.
stops.mistake: Keeping both answers without checking the domain.
stops.reflect: Why can solving correctly still produce an answer that does not work?

stages.desc: A practice check in the same four-equation format as the EL6 CheckIt exercise.

stops.title: Practice check
stops.target: Solve two exponential and two logarithmic equations, giving exact answers. In CheckIt, the two exponential equations share one base and the same two numbers, and so do the two log equations.
stops.cold:
Solve each equation for the variable. Give exact answers.
(a) \(3^{w - 5} = 4\) (b) \(3^n - 5 = 4\) (c) \(7\log_5(2a) = 14\) (d) \(7 + \log_5(2d) = 10\)
stops.coldPlain: Solve each equation, giving exact answers: (a) 3^(w - 5) = 4, (b) 3^n - 5 = 4, (c) 7 log_5(2a) = 14, (d) 7 + log_5(2d) = 10.
stops.coldA:
(a) \(w = \log_3 4 + 5\) (about 6.2619, only to check; CheckIt wants the exact form)[[graph:F1a]](b) \(3^n = 9\), so \(n = \log_3 9\), which simplifies to \(2\). CheckIt may leave it as \(\log_3(9)\); both are correct.
(c) \(a = \tfrac{25}{2}\)[[graph:F1c]](d) \(\log_5(2d) = 3\), \(2d = 125\), \(d = \tfrac{125}{2}\)
stops.solution: (a) The power is alone: w - 5 = log_3 4, so w = log_3 4 + 5. (b) Add 5 first: 3^n = 9, so n = log_3 9 = 2. (c) Divide by 7: log_5(2a) = 2, 2a = 25, a = 25/2. (d) Subtract 7: log_5(2d) = 3, 2d = 125, d = 125/2.
stops.reflect: What is your first move on every one of these equations?
